fetched.purpose: The identity boundary that everything in Azure hangs from.
facts: A tenant is the directory that holds the identities used to sign in and get access. Every Azure subscription trusts exactly one tenant and relies on it to authenticate and authorize users, services and devices.
The person who creates a tenant becomes Global Administrator. A subscription owner who joins their subscription to an existing tenant does not.
Moving a subscription to another tenant breaks role assignments, so AKS clusters lose functionality, and key vault tenant IDs must be changed.

No one has access to the root management group by default; a Global Administrator must elevate access first.
A directory supports 10,000 management groups and a tree up to six levels deep (not counting the root or the subscription level).

fetched.purpose: The control plane every tool (portal, CLI, Terraform) talks to.

cost.note: Listed as free on the Azure free services page.

facts: Every create, update or delete goes through ARM, whichever tool you use. You don't enable it; it is part of the platform.
ARM checks RBAC on every request and evaluates Azure Policy when one is assigned. Role and policy assignments are themselves ARM resources.

Resource providers (Microsoft.Compute, Microsoft.Network, ...) must be registered on a subscription before you use them. Some are registered by default, and the portal and template or Bicep deployments often register them for you. Registering needs the /register/action permission, which Contributor and Owner have.
Terraform's azurerm provider calls ARM's REST API resource by resource and keeps its own state file. It does not generate ARM templates.
Bicep is an Azure-only language that compiles to an ARM template (JSON), which ARM's deployment engine applies. No state file: Azure itself is the record. Preview changes with what-if.

Both describe desired state, but a deployment is one-shot: nothing keeps reconciling afterward (unlike a Kubernetes controller). Drift is found by re-running plan or what-if, or corrected by Azure Policy effects such as DeployIfNotExists.

facts: Three parts: who (principal), what (role), where (scope). Scopes inherit downward.
Contributor manages resources but is not a data role. Use data roles such as Key Vault Secrets User for secrets.

RBAC answers 'who may do what?'. Azure Policy mainly answers 'what is allowed to exist, and how must it be configured?', though policy rules can also look at who makes a request. Full RBAC access does not bypass policy.
A role assignment is its own ARM resource, stored at a scope, so one group assignment can cover many resources. That is why RBAC scales better than per-resource lists.
RBAC is additive: effective permissions are the sum of all assignments that apply. If a deny assignment applies, access is blocked before role assignments are considered.

fetched.purpose: Store secrets, keys and certificates with access control.
facts: Each vault uses one permission model: Azure RBAC (the default and recommended model, and the default for new vaults from API version 2026-02-01) or vault access policies (legacy).

Access policies exist only at the vault level. RBAC roles can be assigned at management group, subscription, resource group, vault, or an individual key, secret or certificate. One vault per application per environment, with roles at vault scope, is recommended over per-object assignments.

Contributor is a management role, but in access-policy mode Contributor and Key Vault Contributor can grant themselves data access by editing an access policy. Read secrets with an RBAC data role such as Key Vault Secrets User, and limit who holds Contributor.
Setting the RBAC permission model invalidates all access policies and can cause outages if equivalent roles are not assigned. Create the role assignments first, then switch and test.

facts: Rules about resource properties and actions. Examples: allowed regions, required tags, diagnostic logs sent to Log Analytics. Rules can also check who makes the request, so policy is not only about configuration.

Assigned at a management group, subscription, resource group or individual resource, and inherited downward; specific scopes can be excluded. It only applies to the resource types and properties its rule matches.

Evaluated when a resource is created or updated, when a policy is newly assigned or changed at a scope, and on a compliance cycle every 24 hours. Effects set the response: deny, log, alter the resource before or after the change, deploy related resources, or block actions. Existing non-compliant resources are not deleted; remediation can fix them.
If a Terraform apply fails with RequestDisallowedByPolicy, read the policy name in the error before debugging the code.

cloud_native_scale.label: Cloud native
cloud_native_scale.description: Built for containers, microservices or event-driven apps: platform-managed scaling, declarative APIs, open standards.

comparisons.title: Observability
comparisons.question: Which monitoring service fits my workload?
comparisons.note: Reviewed against Learn on 2026-10-24. Application Insights is OpenTelemetry-based and Azure Monitor also collects Prometheus metrics, so the audience labels are a simplification: the options overlap.

members.choose_when: The unified service every subscription already has for logs, metrics and alerts across Azure resources. The two options below are parts of it.

members.audience: Workloads that are not cloud native
members.choose_when: Logs and application telemetry in Azure Monitor: KQL queries over workspaces, and Application Insights for application performance monitoring, instrumented with OpenTelemetry. Suits any workload, including VMs and App Service.
Kubernetes metrics: Prometheus for AKS and Azure Arc-enabled clusters with PromQL and Grafana dashboards, when your tooling already speaks Prometheus.

comparisons.title: Compute
comparisons.question: Where should my workload run?
comparisons.note: Drafted from the service purposes already in the model; not yet checked against Microsoft Learn.

members.audience: You want to manage the servers
members.choose_when: Full control of the operating system, or lifting an existing app as it is. Scale sets run groups of identical VMs that scale together.

members.audience: Web apps and APIs, no servers to manage
members.choose_when: A web app or API on a managed platform, without running the servers yourself.
Small pieces of code that run in response to events such as a queue message or a schedule, with no server to run.
You have containers but do not want to operate Kubernetes. Serverless containers that can scale to zero.
You need Kubernetes itself. Azure manages the control plane; you manage the node pools.

cost_scale.label: Free
cost_scale.description: No charge for the service itself. Things you attach to it may cost money.

cost_scale.label: Free tier
cost_scale.description: A permanent free tier or monthly allowance. Free within its limits, billed beyond them.

cost_scale.label: Free for 12 months
cost_scale.description: Free only for new Azure customers during the first 12 months (or on the free credit), billed afterwards.

cost_scale.label: Service free, resources not
cost_scale.description: The service layer is free but running anything on it needs billed resources.

cost_scale.label: Paid
cost_scale.description: No free option found. Usage-based services can still cost only cents for a small lab.
